newsitem.title: CHILE: FEATURE-Chile opens its eyes to rampant child abuse.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Chile opens its eyes to rampant child abuse.

text.p: When 9-month-old Edit Huentecona was rushed to a hospital, her injuries -- burns, a fractured skull, crushed ribs and bruises -- horrified doctors.
Even more shocking was the discovery that the baby's wounds were not an accident but the result of relentless battering by her 16-year-old mother and other relatives.

"Edit was one of the worst cases of child abuse we have seen at this clinic," said Soledad Calves, coordinator of social services at the Doctor Exequiel Gonzalez hospital in Santiago's southern suburbs.

Television pictures of the little girl cowering in the corner of a hospital bed, her face badly burned, outraged Chileans and turned the spotlight on the country's alarmingly high levels of child abuse. The first official glimpse into the scale of the problem was given by a report commissioned by UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund, which said two thirds of Chilean children are victims of physical violence at home, with one third receiving frequent and severe beatings from their parents.

The survey released last year, the first of its kind in Latin America, was based on interviews with 1,500 13-year-old schoolchildren throughout the country. But the study, and a recent rash of headline-grabbing cases like Edit's, do not point to a sudden rise in domestic violence, experts say. Instead, they reflect a greater openness in Chile -- one of Latin America's most conservative countries -- to tackle social taboos like child abuse.
"Child abuse has always existed in Chile. It's a cultural problem which has long been hidden and is now coming out into the light," said Lt. Col. Eugenia Gonzalez of the Carabineros police force.

Despite the extent of the problem, until recently there had not been public discussion of violence in the home. The issue, like other controversial subjects such as divorce and abortion, only started to surface six years ago when Chile returned to democracy after 17 years of military rule.

"These are issues which come out into the open more when a country returns to democracy and people can question authoritarian attitudes,", said psychologist Soledad Larrain of the University of Chile, who led the UNICEF study.

Chile's government is starting to regard child abuse and neglect as a national problem. This year it began a media campaign with posters and TV spots aimed at encouraging parents to be nice to their children. One spot shows a mother and father helping their toddler place eggs into a refrigerator rack. The child drops an egg. Instead of scolding or smacking him, the parents shrug off the incident and give the child another egg and a gentle smile.

Another ad attacks psychological abuse. It shows a boy, about 10, whose body starts vanishing limb by limb as angry voices say, "You're useless," "You're a failure," "You should never have been born." When the child disappears, an announcer says, "Hitting isn't the only way to abuse a child."

The overall incidence of child-battering in Chile appears to be similar to that elsewhere in Latin America. But levels of severe abuse -- including hitting, beating and biting -- are far greater in Chile, UNICEF officials said.
"The level of severe violence which children in Chile suffer is extremely high," Larrain said.

In Chile, more than in some other countries, many parents think the use of violence is a legitimate way of educating and punishing their offspring, she said, adding "It is a very authoritarian society ... and parents have a great degree of power over their children."

Common injuries include bruises, broken jaws, burst eardrums -- the result of children being tugged by their ears -- and cigarette and other burns. Physical violence is more frequent among poorer families. Children of richer parents are more likely to suffer psychological abuse including repeated insults, threats and humiliation, UNICEF said.

The survey did not include sexual abuse, which officials say is one of the most frequent forms of ill-treatment. "It is one of the most important areas of abuse. The problem is it is hard for the children to report and many times they are not believed," Gonzalez said.
Recent changes in the law have given children more protection, but many loopholes remain.

Dressed in a bright red jacket and wooly cap, grinning and gurgling for a reporter in the hospital, little Edit has now mostly recovered from her injuries. But Calves said the girl may have to be returned to her mother if she wants her back.
